lesson_title: The Kettle the Size of a Suburb
hook_text: Somewhere on the Highveld, a kettle the size of a suburb is boiling right now — and your phone is drinking from it.
clip_script: Forget the pylons and the concrete for a moment. A coal power station is the kettle in your kitchen, enlarged until it can boil for sixty million people. Your kettle: an element heats water, steam pushes at the lid. Tutuka or Kendal: coal milled finer than flour burns at one thousand four hundred degrees, and the water sits inside kilometres of steel tubes built into the furnace walls. This steam has no lid to rattle — it slams into the blades of a turbine and spins them three thousand times a minute. On the far end of that spinning shaft sits a huge magnet turning inside coils of copper wire, and that is the entire secret of a generator: spin a magnet in a coil and electricity flows. Transformers then squeeze the voltage up to four hundred thousand volts, because electricity leaks far less energy on a long journey when it travels at high pressure — and Gauteng is a long journey from almost everywhere. Three details to keep. The giant curved towers are coolers, not chimneys — the white clouds are water vapour. The stations sit on the coalfields because a cable is cheaper than a coal train. And the humbling arithmetic: of every three bags of coal that go into the furnace, roughly one bag's worth of energy comes out as electricity. Chemical, heat, spin, spark — that chain is powering your screen right now.
visual_style: A kitchen kettle zooming out step by step until it becomes a Highveld power station; cutaway of flour-fine coal dust igniting, glowing boiler tubes and a whirling magnet in copper coils; a glowing cable racing a slow coal train across a map toward Gauteng; three coal bags with two dissolving into heat haze.
mood: Playful awe turning into quiet astonishment at the scale and the waste.
pacing: Quick zoom-out gag at the open, steady mechanical beat through the energy chain, a held pause on the two lost bags.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and follow the energy from coal seam to phone screen.
